lessons.title: The shape of the South African dairy industry
lessons.html:
Where milk comes from

South African milk is produced on a relatively small number of commercial farms, many with large herds, plus emerging and smallholder producers. Production has shifted strongly towards the coastal regions, where rainfall and pasture growth are more reliable: the Eastern Cape (for example around Tsitsikamma and the Midlands), the Western Cape (especially the southern Cape), and KwaZulu-Natal. Inland provinces such as the Free State, North West and Gauteng have fewer, often larger, operations that rely more on purchased feed.

Production systems

SystemMain features
Pasture-basedCows graze irrigated or dryland ryegrass, kikuyu and clover, with concentrate supplement; lower feed cost, seasonal challenges
Total mixed ration (TMR)Cows housed or in feedlot-style yards, fed mixed rations of silage, hay and concentrates; higher yields, higher costs
Mixed or semi-intensiveGrazing plus a partial mixed ration

Breeds

  • Holstein-Friesian: the largest numbers; high volume.
  • Jersey: smaller, high butterfat and protein, well suited to pasture.
  • Ayrshire and Guernsey: smaller populations.
  • Crossbreds: increasingly used in pasture systems for hardiness and fertility.

The value chain

Milk leaves the farm in bulk tankers to processors who make fresh milk, cheese, yoghurt, butter and milk powder, or is sold by producer-distributors directly. Some producers process on farm. Payment is usually based on volume and components (butterfat, protein) with penalties or bonuses for quality such as somatic cell count and bacterial count.

Industry organisations

Industry bodies include Milk SA, which coordinates industry projects funded by statutory levies; the Milk Producers' Organisation (MPO), representing producers; and the Dairy Standard Agency, which focuses on compliance with food safety and quality standards. Breed societies and milk recording schemes support herd improvement.

lessons.title: Economic, legal and environmental pressures
lessons.html:
Economics of dairy farming

Dairy is a high-cost, low-margin business. Feed is typically the largest cost, followed by labour, and the farm has heavy investments in parlours, cooling, irrigation and vehicles. The milk price is set by buyers and influenced by supply, imports and processing demand, while feed and fuel costs follow grain prices and the rand exchange rate. Many farms have grown larger to stay viable, and the number of producers has fallen over the years.

The key ratio is the milk-to-feed price ratio: how many kilograms of feed one litre of milk can buy. Supervisors influence profitability daily by controlling feed waste, cow health and milk quality.

Legal framework

  • Food safety and hygiene: milk is a foodstuff and the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act 54 of 1972 and its regulations govern hygiene in milking sheds and milk handling. Municipal health officials inspect.
  • Product standards: the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 covers classification and labelling of dairy products.
  • Animal health: the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 controls diseases such as brucellosis and tuberculosis.
  • Medicines and remedies: Act 36 of 1947 for stock remedies; follow labels and veterinary prescriptions, including milk withdrawal periods.
  • Animal welfare: the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.
  • Labour: the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 and sectoral rules for farm workers; the OHS Act 85 of 1993.
  • Water and environment: the National Water Act 36 of 1998 for water use and effluent.

Environmental pressures

  • Drought and erratic rainfall affect pastures and feed prices.
  • Dairy effluent from parlours and yards must be managed to protect water resources.
  • Electricity supply interruptions threaten milking and milk cooling; generators are essential.
  • Heat stress lowers production in summer, especially in high-yielding Holsteins.

Key points

  • Production is concentrated in the Eastern Cape, Western Cape and KwaZulu-Natal.
  • Systems range from pasture-based to TMR.
  • Feed is the largest cost; margins are tight.
  • Milk hygiene, animal health, welfare, labour and water laws all apply.
  • Drought, power cuts, effluent and heat stress are major challenges.
